newsitem.title: PERU: Peru leader said "sorry" to see Cerpa's corpse.
newsitem.headline: Peru leader said "sorry" to see Cerpa's corpse.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Friday he felt "sorry" when he saw the corpse of the guerrilla leader whose seizure of hostages had tormented him for four months.

"For me, I felt sorry not only seeing the body of (Nestor) Cerpa, but also the other youngsters that were dragged into this by him," Fujimori told Reuters in his first interview since Tuesday's military strike against the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers.
Cerpa and his second-in-command Rolly Rojas led a band of 12 other jungle-trained rebels in their teens or early 20s in the MRTA's Dec. 17 storming of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
Cerpa was slain on the staircase of the mansion during Tuesday's commando raid, in which two soldiers and all the other MRTA members also were killed.
Fujimori lingered for a second before stepping past Cerpa's bloodied body during an inspection on Wednesday of the bombed and burned-out residence.
Exhausted but smiling during the interview inside the ornate Government Palace in downtown Lima, Fujimori described the personal strain he felt during the four agonizing months of the hostage siege.
"Undoubtedly, I feel a huge weight off my shoulders, without the heavy responsibility of having in my hands the lives of 72 people," he said.
But the deaths of two soldiers and one of the captives marred his joy at the end of the siege.

"I would be completely satisfied if we had with us the 72 alive. We freed 72, but unfortunately Dr. (Carlos) Giusti died afterwards," he said referring to the Supreme Court judge who received a bullet in the thigh then died of bleeding.

The president said his 16-year-old son, Kenji, and 21-year-old daughter, Keiko, had been his main source of personal solace, especially during the first weeks when he went into seclusion to decide his strategy.
The Fujimori family's personal involvement goes further.

The president's mother and sister were among hundreds of captives released in the first hours after the rebels captured more than 500 cocktail party guests. His brother, Pedro, was among the remaining 71 hostages freed after 126 days in captivity.
And Fujimori himself would probably have been captured at the party had he not been delayed arriving from a visit to the provinces.
Sleeping five hours a day "if I sleep well" and snatching any sleep he could while flying to the provinces and abroad, Fujimori found it difficult to put the crisis out of his mind.
"If ever a space opened up in my mind, this would come in," he said.

After making the decision in principle on Sunday to send the troops in, "I was confident," Fujimori said. "When the television public saw the first images they thought there was going to be a big massacre, but I had seen various trial runs.
"In real dimensions in another place we proved it was effective. So even though it was delicate, I also had a high level of confidence that this strategy was going to work."
He insisted that he made the decision without bowing to pressure.

Fujimori refused to comment on his strongly-suspected ambitions for a third term in Peru's elections in 2000, saying his priority over the next three years was not to consolidate power but "the fight on poverty and under-development."
